notes:
I've written notes for every verse from 1 to 26. I found nothing usable on verses 24–25 apart from one Guzik note, which is under v. 24, or on verses 27–28 themselves. Some points also come only from search-result excerpts, because I could fetch just two full pages (Enduring Word and the Pulpit Commentary).

**Gaps:** I found nothing from Methodist, Lutheran, Pentecostal-denominational (ag.org), Reformed-site or Orthodox sources on this passage. I also found no page on word-of-faith, prosperity or hyper-grace teaching about v. 5. So the "differences between traditions" points below are mostly Protestant versus Catholic, plus differences between individual commentators.

---

**v. 1**
- Ellicott (on BibleHub) says Jesus is walking back into danger, since His life had been threatened on His last visit. Mark may link this visit to the miracles just told, hoping their report had gone ahead of Him. When last He taught in the synagogue of Nazareth, His life had been in danger; and now He thrusts Himself into the wolf's den. Mark seems to wish us to observe the connection between this visit and the great group of miracles which he has just recorded — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-1.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: "his own country" means the Nazareth area, where He grew up though He wasn't born there. Nazareth was about a day's journey from Capernaum, and Luke 4:16 records an earlier visit. Our Lord now left the neighbourhood of Capernaum, and came into His own country — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: they were amazed at His teaching and His signs. But Mark says "many", not all, and the many were envious. The repeated "this man" sounds contemptuous. There is a contemptuous tone about the expression. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm
- Guzik: Jesus left Nazareth a carpenter and came back a rabbi with disciples, so the locals wondered what had happened to Him. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/

**v. 3**
- "Carpenter": Guzik reads it as a put-down meaning He had no formal training, and says the Greek word is broader, closer to "builder". Calling Jesus 'the carpenter' was meant as an insult, reflecting his lack of formal theological training — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/
- Pulpit: Jesus really worked at the trade, probably until His ministry began. Chrysostom says He made ploughs and yokes. Joseph was probably dead by then. We infer from this that our Lord actually worked at the trade of a carpenter, and probably continued to do so until he entered upon his public ministry. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm
- Gill notes that Jewish sayings held carpentry to be an honest trade that went well with learning. for they have a saying (m), that "beautiful is the learning of the law, along with a trade.'' — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-3.htm
- "Son of Mary": Guzik quotes Lane that calling a man after his mother was an insult and may hint at rumours of illegitimacy. "The additional phrase 'the son of Mary' is probably disparaging. It was contrary to Jewish usage to describe a man as the son of his mother, even when she was a widow, except in insulting terms. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/ A commentary on StudyLight disagrees: it sees no slur and thinks Mark is stressing the virgin birth. Mark's record of only this part of their gossip was in all probability for the purpose of stressing the virgin birth. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-3.html
- **The brothers and sisters: the main point where traditions disagree.**
  - *Evangelical/Protestant:* Guzik says This also was not a compliment. about "son of Mary", and on the siblings he concludes that Mary did not stay a virgin after Jesus' birth. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/ Bible.org says Tertullian, Helvidius and most Protestants assert that he was a true half-brother of Jesus by Joseph and Mary — https://bible.org/book/export/html/21427 Barnes says perpetual virginity is not founded on the authority of the Scriptures. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/james.html
  - *Older Protestant commentary that takes the other side:* the Pulpit Commentary lists three views. They were literal brothers; they were Joseph's sons by an earlier marriage (held by many Greek Fathers); or, which it thinks most likely, they were cousins, sons of Mary the wife of Clopas. It points out that the word for "brother" can mean any close relative. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm
  - *Church history:* Schaff (on CCEL) lays out the half-brother theory and the cousin theory, and criticises the half-brother theory as not free of suspicion of an ascetic bias, as being the first step towards the dogma of the perpetual virginity — https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/hcc1.i.IV_1.27.html
  - *Catholic:* the Catholic Encyclopedia argues that the "brethren" were not children of Joseph and Mary. It says the New Testament presents Mary as mother of Jesus alone, and identifies James and Joses as sons of Alphaeus/Clopas and another Mary. It is highly significant that throughout the New Testament Mary appears as the Mother of Jesus and of Jesus alone. — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/02767a.htm Catholic Answers makes a point from this very verse: Nazareth called Him "the son of Mary" (Mark 6:3), not as "*a* son of Mary." — https://www.catholic.com/tract/brethren-of-the-lord
- "Took offense": Chuck Smith (on StudyLight) says the Greek word is "scandalised", that is, they stumbled over Him because they knew Him. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-3.html Guzik: They knew *little enough* about Him to think that they knew *everything* about Him. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/

**v. 4**
- Guzik: Jesus accepted rejection as the price a faithful prophet pays, even though it must have hurt. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/
- Pulpit: people naturally think less of those they grew up with and resent seeing one of their own raised above them. It adds that God abhors the envious, and will withhold the wonders of his grace from those who grudge his gifts to others. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm
- Swindoll (via Precept Austin): hometown people are less likely to applaud someone they knew "back when." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary

**v. 5: "could not" (commentators differ on how to explain it)**
- *Unbelief really limited His work (Guzik, a Calvary Chapel teacher hosted among the Pentecostal/charismatic sites):* This was in respect to God's principle of partnership with man. God may work with *no* belief, but not with *un*belief. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/ The NET Bible's notes agree that Unbelief limits God's working — https://netbible.org/bible/Mark+6
- *His power was not lacking; He chose to hold back (Gill, a Baptist):* the unbelief was not too strong for Christ, who could have removed it but chose not to. not that their unbelief was an over match for his power; he could have removed that, if he had thought fit, but he did not do it — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/6-5.html The BibleHub study note says the inability was moral rather than mechanical. — https://biblehub.com/mark/6-5.htm
- *God does not force belief (Pulpit):* God does not compel conviction once ordinary means have failed, because people's actions must be free if they are to be judged. Nazareth already had enough evidence. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm
- *Faith as the normal condition, with exceptions (Maclaren on BibleHub):* most miracles required faith, but there were exceptions such as the feeding of the thousands. Even here a "trickle" of healing still flowed. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-5.htm
- Expositor's Bible: the phrase shows the fearful power of the human will to resist the will of man's compassionate Redeemer. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/mark/6.htm
- Precept Austin warns against limiting God through unbelief, but also notes that biblical miracles come mainly in clusters (the Exodus, Elijah and Elisha, Christ and the apostles). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62145/
- Matthew Henry: Jesus still did some good there, healing a few, because he is kind even to the evil and unthankful — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_006.cfm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: the word "marvelled" bears on the reality of Christ's human nature. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-6.htm
- Guzik: the only things Jesus is said to marvel at are faith where you wouldn't expect it and unbelief where you wouldn't expect it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/
- NET Bible notes: This is the only time Mark said that Jesus was amazed. — https://netbible.org/bible/Mark+6
- Pulpit: He left Nazareth, apparently never to return, but was not discouraged and offered to others what Nazareth refused. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm

**v. 7**
- Guzik links this to John 20:21: the disciples are sent to do what Jesus did. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/
- Pulpit: Mark mentions only authority over unclean spirits, keeping the focus on Christ's central mission, the fight against Satan. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm

**v. 8**
- Staff or no staff? Matthew and Luke seem to forbid a staff. Pulpit explains that the point is to make no special provision: whoever had a staff could use it, but no one should go and get one. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm Matthew Henry instead says the staff forbidden elsewhere was a fighting staff, while Mark allows a walking staff, such as pilgrims carried. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_006.cfm
- Guzik: travelling light kept them dependent on God. He also mentions a rabbinic rule against entering the temple with a staff, shoes or money bag. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/
- Pulpit: Mark's word for money is "brass" (copper), chosen for Roman readers. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: covered shoes are forbidden, but open sandals that protect the soles on rocky ground are allowed. Acts 12:8 shows Peter wearing sandals. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: they should not switch lodgings, so as not to seem restless or offend their first hosts, and should not stay so long that they became a burden. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik: Jews shook off dust when leaving Gentile towns, so a Jewish town that rejected the message was to be treated like a Gentile one. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/
- Pulpit: the dust showed they had come, delivered the message and been refused. It also notes that the "Sodom and Gomorrah" clause found in some Bibles is missing from the best manuscripts. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm
- Precept Austin: They were free to walk away with a clear **conscience**, knowing they had done all they could do. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: preaching repentance was their main work; the miracles served it. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm
- Matthew Henry: repentance meant changing their minds and reforming their lives because the Messiah's kingdom was near. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_006.cfm
- Guzik quotes Morgan: they preached in a way that produced repentance. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/

**v. 13: anointing with oil (Protestants and Catholics differ)**
- *Medicine and sign:* Barnes says oil was commonly used for the sick and had a soothing effect. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-13.htm Guzik says oil pictured the Holy Spirit but may also have been medicine. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/
- *Gill says the opposite:* the oil was a sign, not a medicine, otherwise there would have been no miracle in the cure — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-13.htm
- Expositor's notes that the apostles anointed with oil as St. James afterwards directed, but as Jesus never did. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/mark/6.htm
- *Protestant objection to the sacrament:* Pulpit says neither this verse nor James 5 supports "extreme unction", because in both cases the sick got better, while that rite is given just before death. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm Gill (on StudyLight) argues the same way. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kja/mark/6-13.html
- *Catholic:* Catholic Answers says Mark here refers to the sacrament of Anointing of the Sick. Quoting the Catechism, it says the sacrament is alluded to indeed by Mark, but is recommended to the faithful and promulgated by James the apostle — https://www.catholic.com/tract/anointing-of-the-sick

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: this is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great and tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea. He abandoned the daughter of King Aretas for Herodias. Following Chrysostom and Augustine, it says Herod concluded that John had risen in the person of Jesus. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm
- Guzik: Augustus refused Antipas the title "king"; Mark uses it either as local custom or ironically. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/
- Bengel: Except for the public rumour, Herod would not have known of Him. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-14.htm

**v. 15**
- Guzik: people guessed Elijah because of Malachi 4:5, or "the Prophet" because of Deuteronomy 18:15. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/

**v. 16**
- Guzik: Herod's confusion came from a guilty conscience. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/
- Benson: The suggestions of his guilty conscience were too powerful to be removed by the flattery of his servants — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/6-14.htm
- Pulpit: belief in the transmigration of souls may have influenced him, and he was perhaps contradicting his own Sadducee views. It quotes Chrysostom: Herod fears John "even though dead". — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm

**v. 17**
- Pulpit, citing Josephus: the prison was the fortress of Machaerus, where John was beheaded. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm

**v. 18**
- Pulpit: the Greek tense means John warned Herod repeatedly. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm
- Matthew Henry: faithful ministers must not be afraid of the face of man. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_006.cfm
- Guzik: John did not spare the rich and powerful. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/

**v. 19**
- Pulpit squares this with Matthew 14:5, where Herod wants John dead: Herod wanted to kill him at first, but John gradually gained influence over him. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm

**v. 20**
- Text: Pulpit says the best manuscripts read "he was much perplexed", not "he did many things" (KJV). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm
- Precept Austin: "kept him safe" describes ongoing protection, and ironically prison was the safest place from Herodias. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary
- Guzik quotes Lane: Herod was "More weak than cruel — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/
- Matthew Henry: "just and holy" means justice toward people and holiness toward God. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_006.cfm

**v. 21**
- Precept Austin: the third group of guests suggests the feast was at Tiberias, though Machaerus would be a striking setting. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary

**v. 22**
- Pulpit: the Greek stresses that it was Herodias's own daughter who danced, not a hired dancing-girl. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm
- Guzik, quoting Robertson and Trapp: such dancing was almost unheard of for a woman of rank. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/

**v. 24**
- Guzik: Herodias's instant answer shows she had planned it. Robertson thinks the girl wasn't expecting her mother's grim reply. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/

**v. 26**
- Pulpit: Herod's grief was real, but he thought a king's word was law, though he must have known an oath to do evil didn't bind him. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/6.htm
- Guzik quotes Wessel: the word for "consumed with sorrow" is the one used of Jesus in Gethsemane (Mark 14:34). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-6/
- Hiebert (via Precept Austin) blames moral cowardice, and the commentary concludes that the guilt for John's beheading fell on Herod's head! — https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-6-commentary
